Design 3 now gives the test (confidence with a named basis; recovery cost cheap, costly or irreversible; a table of what to do with each pair; a never-delegated list; re-flagging as a decision's dependents grow, since recovery cost rises over time; an overturn flow that applies the recorded undo) and its tradeoffs. commits.summary: example-targets positive P3: 307's claim, oracle, driver, probes and US-ASCII mutant
commits.body:
Example 307 (Spring Security fe9e4549, BCrypt.hashpw(String,String) moving from getBytes("UTF-8") to getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) gets its packet. claims/hashpw-preservation.json, in workflow W1's example-target-claim/v1 format, freezes the domain. The password is null or at most 80 UTF-16 code units of any values. The salt is one of seven fixed strings from upstream's BCryptTests: the 'abc' test vector's cost-6 salt and its stored hash, the $2$05$ salt, and null, empty, cost-03 and too-short salts. The claim observes the returned String or the exception's class. The brief's three domain decisions are explicit: a null password (NullPointerException), malformed surrogates (encoded as '?', as String.getBytes specifies) and invalid salts (IllegalArgumentException) are all in the domain. Exception messages are excluded, because since JDK 14 an NPE's message names the method the patch changes.

replay/probes.json has 45 probes, among them 71, 72 and 73 UTF-8 bytes in 1- to 4-byte characters and a character straddling byte 72, plus three upstream known answers. controls/oracle.py computes no cipher. It encodes UTF-8 itself, and predicts that probes with the same salt and the same first 72 bytes of bcrypt's cyclic key share a result; that distinct keys give distinct results is a stated assumption. That makes the encoding observable, also against the stored hash. The driver passes arguments as UTF-16 code units. The mutant controls/us-ascii.patch (sha256 a2b4e97f...) is on after. target.json gains the claim, the controls and two predicted blockers (java-semantics, input-construction); README and example.json describe the packet.

Verified by hand, as notes, not evidence. Each commit's BCrypt.java was compiled alone with javac 8, and Central's spring-security-crypto 5.2.0.RELEASE (sha1 checked) was run beside them. All three agree with the oracle and with each other on all 45 probes, byte-identically on JDK 21 and 25. The mutant breaks the oracle 9 times and differs on 17 non-ASCII probes. javap shows before and after differ only in hashpw(String,String), apart from constant-pool indices. A jvmcontract gaps scan (records/hashpw-gaps.json) refuses the changed conversion itself on both sides (getBytes(String), getBytes(Charset), StandardCharsets.UTF_8), plus Arrays.copyOf, Integer.parseInt and StringBuilder.charAt in the callee. W1's planner, run from a temporary copy of wqsyopql, plans both tasks. The targets suite (41), test_build.py (190), the contract (16, 13 skipped) and build.py --plan pass. Progress names P5 (example 105) as next; the brief is otherwise accurate.

commits.summary: example-targets runtime R1: source locks and the fixture route's preparation
commits.body: The runtime stream's first piece (llm-dlc/loops/example-targets-runtime.md, R1). runtime.lock(plan, revision) is new and offline: it returns a PreparedTarget at source-locked, with every selected source, adapter, driver and oracle path inside the example's folder (symlinks included) and hashed, and nothing fetched or built. runtime.prepare() now implements the fixture route: it compiles with build_fixtures.py's recipe (--release 21, a fixed JAR date, sorted entries) using the JDK build_fixtures.py would use, resolved to its real home, so the original JAR is byte for byte build_fixtures.py's. It records the original, adapter, driver and oracle by sha256, the ordered classpath, the JDK identity (release file and java -version), the loaded target's origin, and writes prepared.json to the work directory. It returns failed, with its stage, diagnostic and whatever artifacts exist, for a class held by more than one classpath entry (shadowing), a target method the original doesn't declare, an adapter that never references the target method, a compile failure, sources changed between lock and build, and a work directory that isn't an earlier preparation's (left alone). The published-artifact and upstream-build routes return Unsupported until R2. New modules runtime_jdk.py (installed JDKs by full path) and runtime_jar.py (a small class-file reader).

commits.summary: example-targets runtime R4: each fixture revision's controls in its own JVM, per JDK
commits.body:
runtime.run_controls() replaces Phase 0's stub. Each revision's driver runs in its own JVM on its prepared classpath, on each JDK the artifact entry names (21 and 25 for the fixture), selected by full path, with the oracle's PROBES as inputs. The JVM gets a fixed environment (C.UTF-8, UTC, en-US, UTF-8 streams) and inherits nothing from the caller, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and CLASSPATH included. Each raw ExecutionRecord names the JDK (java -version, home, release file), the commit, each classpath entry's sha256 and role, the driver, the inputs' source and hash, and whether this is original-JVM or model replay. Before any JVM starts, the classpath bytes are rechecked against the preparation. A revision that is unprepared, failed or stale, a missing JDK, or a JDK too old for the class files gives a not-started record, never a skipped one. A kill, a timeout, malformed output, or inputs missing or out of order give no observations; exit 1 with complete output stays raw. Nothing here applies the oracle.

Verified inline: contract A3/A4 pass (contract: 8 pass, 8 skip: 6 at workflow's stubs, A5's 2 for want of a built jvmcontract). test_runtime.py has 28 tests, among them the kill (signal 9), timeout, malformed, incomplete and exit-1 drivers, a one-sided pair, stale bytes and the inherited-options check. llm-dlc/tools/example-targets-integration.sh exits 0 (targets suite 68, test_build 190, test_pipeline 29).

Brief note: PreparedTarget carries no work directory. run_controls therefore finds a preparation by route.py's layout and checks its prepared.json. An additive field is recorded as an interface request under Progress.

commits.summary: example-targets runtime R2: the published-artifact route, hash-pinned acquisition and a rechecked cache
commits.body: runtime.lock() and prepare() now take route: published-artifact. The lock stays offline. It records the revision's commit as unchecked release linkage, and the JAR and each declared dependency (in classpath order) by fixed coordinates, an allowed URL and a recorded sha256. A dynamic version, a missing hash, a host other than Maven Central or github.com, and a Central URL naming another file are lock blockers. The new runtime_maven.py (stdlib only, so it runs under python3 -I) acquires each JAR from a content-addressed cache that rechecks every restore and moves a corrupt entry aside. On a miss it fetches into a new empty directory and checks the bytes against the lock before caching or using them. A mismatch fails at acquire and is never cached or rebuilt. It fetches only when the plan's network flag allows. The cache log stays out of the PreparedTarget, so a cache hit is reuse, not identity. Every failed preparation now carries source.blocker (stage, command, diagnostic, needed semantics, next action). A missing hash points at 'runtime_maven.py pin G:A:V', which records it after checking Maven Central's .sha1.

commits.summary: example-targets runtime R5: the vertical slice on PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch from published spring-core
commits.body:
runtime_slice.py takes one small published upstream method end to end, with runtime_simplematch/ as its case folder (not an example and not in the router; its plan uses 315, from the runtime range). The method is org.springframework.util.PatternMatchUtils#simpleMatch(String,String) from spring-core 5.3.18 and 5.3.19. The sidecar is a valid example-target/v1. It names the release tags by full commit, checked with git ls-remote on github.com. It pins each release's spring-core JAR and spring-jcl (spring-core's one compile dependency, per its POM at that version) by Maven Central URL and sha256. runtime_maven.py pin recorded each sha256 and checked it against Central's .sha1. The adapter only calls the method. The driver reads each input as a JSON pair of strings or nulls and prints the raw outcome. The oracle is written from the Javadoc, not the code: 45 probes over nulls, every pattern style, adjacent stars, backtracking, case, a line break, regex metacharacters and a non-BMP character.

The path: the sidecar becomes the TaskPlan asked of workflow's W1, then runtime.prepare (hash-checked acquisition and cache, the adapter and driver built, the classpath checked for shadowing and the target method), then run_controls (each release in its own JVM on JDK 21 and 25), then workflow.ingest, called as route.run calls it. Ingestion is still W2's stub, so it answers Unsupported.

Verified inline. The slice was run from an empty cache (the 4 JARs fetched from Central and checked) and again --offline: both releases artifacts-ready, the target loaded from the spring-core JAR, 4 records each exited 0 with 45 observations and no oracle problems, and JDK 21 and 25 agree on each release. test_runtime.py has 43 tests, 4 new: the sidecar validates and both releases lock offline; offline with an empty cache, preparation is an acquire blocker with its command and next action; the oracle rejects five plausible wrong implementations, and a missing probe raises; the end-to-end slice runs from a private copy of the cache entries (skipped, not faked, without them). The integration script exits 0: contract 8 pass and 8 skip, targets suite 83 (the end-to-end slice ran), test_build 190, test_pipeline 29.

Progress also records two things for review. First, PatternMatchUtils.class is byte-identical in the two releases: the CVE-2022-22968 fix changed DataBinder. Second, a note on what 105's migration needs from runtime: the recorded PR pair isn't released, so it needs the upstream-build route (Maven) or a release pair the positive stream would have to justify; the historical single-file javac compile would be an extracted source slice, not original bytecode; the method is int-only with no dependencies, and its controls can run on JDK 21 and 25. Next: R3's run_verifier, then the upstream-build route as a job.

commits.summary: example-targets runtime R3: run_verifier, jvmcontract on the prepared original artifacts (verification pending)
commits.body:
runtime.run_verifier replaces Phase 0's stub. A prove task runs jvmcontract prove on its revision's original JAR, with its dependencies in classpath order and the claim's assume, assert, throws, nullable and may-alias. An equivalence task runs jvmcontract equivalence between the pair's originals, --unchanged-unless the allowed change. Both get the plan's explicit --engine and --gaps, the claim's bounds, its plan and contracts files (rechecked by sha256) and --json. The run uses a fixed environment with JDK 25 by full path. The result is one raw verifier ExecutionRecord. Its identities record the jvmcontract digest, the JDK, each revision's classpath and commit, a scope label with the loaded class and its origin, models and assumptions, and a capability probe (jvmcontract gaps, a static scan). A one-sided pair, stale bytes or a preparation that isn't ready gives a not-started record. A kill, a timeout or output that isn't the --json outcome gives no observations. What can't be attempted as stated is Unsupported: a replay task, a missing engine, claim models, a changed claim file, differing dependency closures, or no jvmcontract.

Found while dry-running: the fixture's regex-probe failed preparation, because its adapter calls Gate, not RegexGate, so after the merge contract A5's regex-probe row would have failed on runtime's adapter check. Only a replay task's adapter must now call the target. A proof task records the original methods its adapter calls, and run_controls doesn't run controls whose adapter doesn't call the task's target. A plan entry naming a constructed mutant (workflow's W1) is now Unsupported in lock, never prepared as its base. A proof is read from the verifier's --json outcome with build.py's rules: exit 1 alone is invalid output, a violation needs its witness, a refusal is unresolved.
